summary: This experimental document describes a resolver discovery service for URNs implemented with a new DNS record, NAPTR, which gives rules for mapping parts of URIs to domain names. It was replaced by RFCs 3401 through 3404.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2168 describes NAPTR, a DNS record that says how to turn part of a name into the next name to look up. A client starts with the scheme or namespace of the identifier, looks up the matching NAPTR records, and follows the rewrite they carry until it reaches a record naming a server that can answer the real question.

questions: what is urn resolution using dns
subtitle: A DNS record type that lets a client find the server that knows how to turn a name into an address.

tldr.problem: A URL names both a host and a path, so there is no graceful way to move the resource to a different host or to have it served from several places once the URL has been handed out.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC introduces the NAPTR record type, whose fields hold a rewrite rule. A client looks up a name built from the URI's prefix, applies the rewrite to get the next name to query, and repeats until it reaches a terminal record that points at a resolver.
tldr.outcome: The record also allows several services to be offered for the same name and, with the SRV record, allows the resolvers themselves to be replicated. It was replaced by RFCs 3401 to 3404.

facts.label: Resolution services
facts.value: N2L, N2Ls, N2R, N2Rs, N2C, N2Ns, L2R, L2Ns, L2Ls, L2C

today: RFC 2168 has been obsoleted by RFC 3401 and the related documents RFC 3402, RFC 3403 and RFC 3404, so it is no longer a current standards document. It was published in June 1997 as an Experimental protocol, and RFC 2915 later updated it.

sections.title: Why a Resolver Discovery Service
sections.content:
Uniform Resource Locators are the foundation of the World Wide Web and a vital Internet technology, but they have proven brittle in practice. A URL typically identifies a particular path to a file on a particular host, so there is no graceful way of changing the path or host once the URL has been assigned, and no graceful way of replicating the resource to get better network use or fault tolerance. Uniform Resource Names were proposed as an adjunct to URLs that would overcome such problems, and both are instances of the broader class of identifiers called Uniform Resource Identifiers.

The requirement document for URN resolution systems defines the concept of a resolver discovery service, and this document describes the first, experimental, one. The compromise reached in a series of meetings between the developers of several proposals, known as the Knoxville framework, had one major principle: the resolution system must be separate from the way names are assigned, in marked contrast to most URLs, which identify the host to contact and the protocol to use. Separating the two lets multiple naming approaches and resolution approaches compete, and lets different protocols and resolvers be used. There is one problem with the separation: how do you resolve a name when the name cannot give you directions to its resolver?

For the short term, DNS is the obvious candidate for the resolution framework, since it is widely deployed and understood. But DNS is not appropriate for holding information on a per-resource basis. DNS was never intended to handle that many records, its limited record size is wrong for catalog information, and domain names are not suitable as URNs. So the approach here is to use DNS to locate resolvers that can provide information on individual resources, possibly including the resource itself.

The RFC is candid about why the work was published as Experimental rather than as a standards-track document. URN resolution was new to the IETF and the group wanted operational experience first. The proposal is based on DNS and inherits its concerns about security and administration, which the advance of DNSSEC and secure update reduced but did not remove. There was also concern about a noticeable impact on the DNS, since the proposal relies on caching and on additional information. The rewrite rules are based on regular expressions, which are difficult for humans to construct correctly and are especially awkward for international character sets. Finally, the requirements document for URN resolution services was not yet complete, and the RFC says it needs to precede any resolution service proposal on the standards track.
sections.plainLanguage: A URL bakes the address into the name, so moving the file or adding a mirror means breaking the link. The fix is to split the name from the place it can be found, and to have a directory say where the place is. DNS is the obvious place to keep that directory, because everyone already runs it.

sections.title: The NAPTR Record Fields
sections.content:
The NAPTR record is written as Domain, TTL, Class, Order, Preference, Flags, Service, Regexp and Replacement, and its DNS type code is 35.

The order field is a 16-bit integer giving the order in which the records must be processed, so that correct delegation of portions of a namespace works. Low numbers go first, and once a NAPTR is found that matches a URI, the client must not consider any NAPTR with a higher order value. The preference field is also a 16-bit integer, and gives the order among records that share the same order value. It works like the preference field of an MX record, so administrators can direct clients towards more capable hosts or lighter protocols.

The flags field holds single characters from A to Z and 0 to 9, with the case of the letters not significant. Three are defined. S means the next lookup should be for SRV records rather than NAPTR records, A means the next lookup should be for A records, and P means the remainder of the resolution is carried out in a protocol-specific way and no more DNS queries should be made. The S, A and P flags are mutually exclusive, and a resolution library may signal an error if more than one is given. Implementers must not assume the field holds only one character, because multiple flags are anticipated in the future. A client that meets an unknown flag must ignore that record and move to the next one, and this test takes precedence even over the order field.

The service field names the resolution protocol and the resolution services available down this rewrite path. A protocol must be given if the flags say the record is terminal, and if a protocol is given but the flags do not say the record is terminal, the next lookup must be for a NAPTR. The field is an optional protocol followed by zero or more resolution services, each marked with a plus sign. The empty string is valid, which is what is seen at the top of a namespace where the services on offer cannot yet be known. The known protocol strings are rcds, hdl, thttp, rwhois and z3950.

The regexp field holds a substitution expression applied to the original URI to construct the next domain name to look up, and is the core concept of the record. It should be used when the next domain name depends on information in the URI. The replacement field is the other way to express the rewrite, and is the right choice when the next domain name is fixed; if the rewrite is more than a simple substitution of a domain name, the replacement field should be set to a single dot and the regexp field used. The developers believe regexps should rarely be needed, since the replacement field is adequate for the vast majority of situations; regexps are necessary only when portions of a namespace are delegated to different resolvers. The two fields are mutually exclusive at present, though developers should be aware that a future flag might require values in both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each NAPTR record carries six things: which records to try first, which to prefer among equals, what to look up next, what service is on offer, and two ways of writing the rewrite rule. The simple way is a fixed next name; the powerful way is a pattern that picks the next name out of the URI.

sections.title: The Resolution Procedure
sections.content:
Resolution always starts the same way. The start of the URI is scanned to extract its colon-delimited prefix; for a URN the prefix is always urn: and the namespace identifier that follows is extracted. The extracted string is appended to the well-known suffix .urn.net, and DNS is queried for NAPTR records at that name. Depending on the results, zero or more further DNS queries may be needed to locate a resolver. The details of the conversation between the client and the resolver are outside the bounds of the document.

To keep the rewrite rules understandable, NAPTR rules are always applied to the original URI and never to the output of previous rules. The general case may need several rewrites to find a resolver, but eventually there is a terminal NAPTR. Once there is one, the next probe into DNS is for an SRV or an A record rather than another NAPTR. Rather than probing for a NAPTR that does not exist in order to end the loop, the flags field says that the lookup is terminal.

The RFC's first example uses a URN in the hypothetical DUNS namespace, where the identifier is a number for a registered business, giving a URN of the form urn:duns:002372413:annual-report-1997. The namespace identifier duns is extracted, put in front of urn.net, and the NAPTRs for duns.urn.net are looked up. They might return three records with the same order value, so no delegation order has to be followed, and different preference values, so that the provider would prefer the dunslink protocol, then RCDS, with HTTP as a last resort. The service fields say that dunslink can answer either an N2L or an N2C request, that RCDS can answer an N2C, and that HTTP can answer N2L, N2C or N2R. All three records name the next domain to query, so none needs a regular expression.

All three records carry the s flag, so the lookup is terminal. Assuming the client does not know the dunslink protocol, its next action is to look up SRV records for the given name, which name the hosts that can provide the resolution service and the port to use. There is an opportunity for significant optimisation here, because the SRV records can be returned as additional information for terminal NAPTRs, and the A records as additional information for those SRVs. With a long time to live for the .urn.net records, the average number of DNS probes needed to resolve a URN would approach one, so DNS server implementors should provide additional information with NAPTR responses.

The second example uses a URN in a namespace based on MIME Content-Ids, of the form urn:cid:199606121851.1@mordred.gatech.edu. Here the replacement field is empty and the rewrite comes from a regular expression, which extracts the domain part of the identifier. Because the flags do not say the lookup is terminal, the next probe is for more NAPTR records at the extracted name, which is where the provider's list of resolvers is found, with the s flag marking the end of the NAPTR chain.

The third example shows the mechanism working for URLs that have already been handed out. The prefix http is extracted and NAPTR records are looked up for http.urn.net, which rewrite the URL to extract the host name; looking up NAPTR records for that host name then gives the mirror sites, and an SRV lookup on those names tells the client which hosts foo.com has designated and the port to use, so the client can pick one.
sections.plainLanguage: The client takes the first part of the name, looks it up in DNS, and gets back a rule telling it what to look up next. It keeps doing that until a rule says the lookup is finished, at which point DNS gives it a host and a port to talk to.

sections.title: The Resolution Services
sections.content:
The service field names an optional protocol followed by zero or more resolution services, each marked with a plus sign. The services themselves are named by short codes, and their behaviour is described in a separate URN resolution services document; the RFC lists them in brief.

The N-prefixed services all start from a URN. N2L returns a URL, N2Ls returns a set of URLs, N2R returns an instance of the resource, N2Rs returns multiple instances of the resource, typically encoded using multipart/alternative, N2C returns a collection of meta-information on the named resource, and N2Ns returns all the URNs that are also identifiers for the resource. The L-prefixed services start from a URL instead: L2R returns the resource, L2Ns returns all the URNs that are identifiers for the resource, L2Ls returns all the URLs for instances of the same resource, and L2C returns a description of the resource.

The actual format of a service request and response is determined by the resolution protocol, and is the subject of other documents. Protocols need not offer every service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each service is one question you can ask a resolver: give me the address, give me the file, give me a description, give me the other names for this thing. The first letter says which way round the question is, URN to something or something to URN.

sections.title: Notes for Implementers and Administrators
sections.content:
The notes for implementers are firm about ordering. A client must process multiple NAPTR records in the order given by the order field and must not simply use the first record that offers a known protocol and service combination. If a record at a particular order matches the URI but the client does not know the protocol or the service, the client should continue examining records with the same order, and must not consider records with a higher order value. This is what makes delegation of portions of a namespace work, letting a site administrator say that all requests for URIs matching one pattern go to one server and all others to another. A record counts as a match if it supplies a replacement domain name or if its regular expression matches the URI.

Where several records share an order value, the preference field is used to pick the next one to consider, though clients may use different criteria such as preferred protocols, network distance or bandwidth. If a lookup after a rewrite fails, clients are strongly encouraged to report the failure rather than backing up to pursue other rewrite paths. When a namespace is delegated among a set of resolvers, regexps must be used, each in a separate NAPTR record, and administrators should do as little delegation as possible because of limits on the size of DNS responses.

For domain administrators the RFC has a warning about regular expressions. They are hard to get right on their own, and any backslashes in a regexp must be entered twice in a zone file in order to appear once in a query response, which not every DNS server implementor has handled correctly. Only when delegating portions of namespaces should the typical administrator need regexps at all. There is also a warning about the shell, where a backslash is a common escape character, so what looks like an escaped backslash may not be one.

The substitution expression grammar is given in full. The first character of the expression is the delimiter and there must be exactly three unescaped occurrences of it; digits must not be used as delimiters, because backreferences would then be confused with literal digits. The pattern part is a POSIX Extended Regular Expression and the replacement part may contain backreferences, where a digit from 1 to 9 refers to the correspondingly numbered parenthesised group in the pattern. The i flag makes the matching case-insensitive. The result of applying the expression to the original URI must be a string that obeys the syntax for DNS host names, and client software should verify that before querying it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules matter to anyone writing these records. First, work through them in the order given, because that is what makes delegation work. Second, avoid the pattern form unless you really need it: it is hard to write, hard to read, and the escaping rules differ between a zone file and what a client receives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The use of urn.net as the registry for URN namespaces is subject to denial of service attacks and to other DNS spoofing attacks. The interactions with DNSSEC were being studied at the time of writing, and it was expected that NAPTR records would be signed with SIG records once the DNSSEC work was deployed.

The rewrite rules make identifiers from other namespaces subject to the same attacks as ordinary domain names. Since those identifiers had not been easily resolvable before, the RFC says this may or may not be considered a problem.

Regular expressions should be checked for sanity, not passed blindly to something like Perl.

Finally, the RFC has discussed only how to locate a resolver, not how the conversation with that resolver takes place. There are significant security considerations attached to that conversation, and they are outside the scope of this document and must be addressed by the specifications for the particular resolver communication protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry of namespace names lives in DNS, so it inherits DNS's weaknesses, including the possibility of an attacker answering with a false name. And once the resolver has been found, everything that follows depends on the protocol used to talk to it, which this RFC leaves to other documents.

messages.label: NAPTR query for duns.urn.net
messages.note: The namespace identifier from the URI is appended to the .urn.net suffix.

messages.label: NAPTR records
messages.note: Each record names the next domain to query and the services available down that path.

messages.label: NAPTR query for the rewritten name
messages.note: The rewrite rule from the first record produces the next name to look up.

messages.label: Terminal NAPTR
messages.note: A record whose flags say the next lookup is for SRV or A records.

messages.label: SRV query
messages.note: The terminal record names the domain whose SRV records list the resolvers.

messages.label: SRV records
messages.note: They name the hosts that can do the resolution and the port to use.

viz.caption: THE SIX FIELDS OF A NAPTR RECORD

items.title: Order
items.text: A 16-bit number giving the order in which records must be processed, so that delegation of parts of a namespace works. Low numbers first.

items.title: Preference
items.text: A 16-bit number giving the order among records that share the same order value, so that clients prefer more capable hosts.

items.title: Flags
items.text: Single characters that say what the next lookup should be: S for SRV records, A for A records, P for protocol-specific.

items.title: Service
items.text: The resolution protocol and the resolution services available down this rewrite path.

items.title: Regexp
items.text: A substitution expression applied to the original URI to construct the next domain name to look up.

items.title: Replacement
items.text: A fixed next name to query, used instead of a pattern when the rewrite does not depend on the URI.
